name: Jarmā al-Kubrā
history:
The manuscript reading 'حرمى' (Harmā) is a classic Arabic scribal dotting error (iʿjām omission) for 'جرمى' (Jarmā), representing Greek Γάραμα μητρόπολις (Garama Metropolis) recorded in Ptolemy's Geography (Book IV). Garama was the royal capital of the Garamantes civilization. The classical latitude of 19° N represents an astronomical compression into Clime 1, while the 26° longitude minus 17.5° yields 8.5° E, about 4.6° west of Germa’s true longitude (13°04′ E); the table below lists the site’s modern position, not the converted value.

Garama was the northern gateway and primary oasis emporium of the Central Trans-Saharan Trade Route. It controlled the foggaras (subterranean irrigation channels) that sustained caravan traffic carrying gold dust, ostrich feathers, salt, and exotic animals from Sub-Saharan Africa to the Mediterranean ports of Oea (Tripoli), Sabratha, and Leptis Magna.
idrisiHint: Navigate to Clime 1, Section 3. Look inland south of the Mediterranean coast of Tripoli into the Fezzan desert corridor.

name: Mamlakat al-Ḥabasha
history:
Mamlakat al-Ḥabasha refers to the ancient Aksumite/Abyssinian Christian kingdom centered on the Tigray plateau and Eritrean highlands. A printed latitude of 19° N (يط) places the realm inside Clime 1, with the northern frontier of Abyssinian influence adjoining Nubia and the Red Sea littoral.

Served as the crucial hinge between the African interior and the Red Sea trade. Aksumite merchants exported ivory, gold, frankincense, myrrh, emeralds, and civet through the historic Red Sea port of Adulis, exchanging them for Byzantine glass, Roman wine, Indian spices, and silks.
idrisiHint: Located in Clime 1, Sections 4 and 5. Find Bilād al-Ḥabasha positioned south (higher on the sheet) of Nubia and the Beja lands.

name: Dunqula min Bilād al-Nūba
history:
Old Dongola was the fortified royal capital of the Christian Nubian kingdom of Makuria (al-Muqurra) from the 6th to 14th centuries CE. In Arab geographical tradition, it is the premier urban center of Nubia, established firmly within Clime 1.

Dongola commanded the major north-south riverine trade along the Nile as well as desert bypass routes leading to the Red Sea port of Aidhab (ʿAydhāb) and the western desert tracks (Wadi Howar, Darb al-Gallāba) that linked Dongola with the Darfur–Kharga–Asyut road, the Darb al-Arbaʿīn proper, which itself did not pass through Dongola. Under the historic Baqṭ treaty, Dongola exported cattle, gold, ebony, and ivory to Egypt in exchange for Mediterranean wheat, oil, textiles, and fine pottery.
idrisiHint: Located in Clime 1, Section 4. Trace the Nile River from the top downwards; Dunqula is prominently inscribed on the major bend of the river.

name: Kūshah al-Wāghilah
history:
The manuscript phrase 'كوص وواعلة منه' is proposed here (the journal’s own conjecture, unsourced) to be an unpointed scribal degradation of 'كوشة الواغلة' (Kūshah al-Wāghilah — 'Kush the Inland/Remote'). It preserves the ancient name of Kush/Cush and the Nile cataract settlement of Kosha, situated at 20°45′ N, about 45′ north of the Ikhwān’s 20° N and 15′ above the limit of Clime I (20°30′).

Kosha lies on the left (west) bank of the Nile in the Third Cataract region of Northern Sudan.

name: Saqlī / Simylla (Chaul)
history:
The reading 'سقلي' (Saqlī) is proposed here, as the journal’s own conjecture, to be an Arabic transcription of Greek Σίμυλλα (Simylla / Semylla) from Ptolemy's Geography (Book VII) and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (Cemūla in two inscriptions). Transliterated into unpointed Arabic script, Sīmullā corrupted to Saqlī. Sialkot in Punjab (32°30′ N) is too far north for Clime 1 and non-maritime, whereas Chaul lies at 18°33′ N, 33′ north of the printed 18° N.

Chaul/Simylla was one of the greatest international deep-water emporia on the western seaboard of India (Konkan coast). It received ships arriving across the Arabian Sea from Oman, Aden, and the Persian Gulf laden with Arabian thoroughbred horses, dates, and frankincense, exporting Indian black pepper, teakwood, semi-precious stones, and fine muslins.
idrisiHint: Found in Clime 1, Section 8. Look along the western coastal strip of India south of the Gulf of Cambay and the Indus mouth.

name: al-Mayd min al-Sind
history:
The Meds (al-Mayd) were an ancient seafaring, pastoral, and coastal population native to the lower Indus delta and Makran coast (identified with the Ichthyophagi of classical Greek records). Arab chroniclers (Ibn Hawqal, al-Istakhri, al-Idrisi) document them controlling the coastal lagoons from Gwadar to Kutch.

The Meds dominated maritime transport, pilotage, and coastal cabotage between Makran, the port of Daybul, and the Gulf of Cambay. They were renowned both as skilled maritime navigators and as naval corsairs who controlled the coastal choke points of the northern Arabian Sea.
idrisiHint: Located in Clime 1 & 2, Section 8. Look along coastal pastures west and south of the Indus River between Tīz in Makran and Daybul/Mansura in Sindh.

name: ʿUmān (Dhofar)
history:
The manuscript phrase 'عمان من بلاد الغرب' contains an unpunctuated boundary between the southern Arabian catalog (Dhofar, Mahra, Oman) and the Western/African list. An Ikhwān latitude of 18° N specifically pinpoints Southern Oman (Dhofar/Zafār), whereas northern Oman (Muscat/Sohar) lies at ~23°36′ N in Clime 2.

Dhofar was the uncontested global center of the Frankincense Trade (the Land of Frankincense). Its ancient ports (Sumhuram/Khor Rori, Mirbat, Al-Baleed) gathered resin harvested from the Boswellia sacra trees of the Dhofar mountains, shipping it across the Indian Ocean to India, Egypt, Rome, and Mesopotamia.
idrisiHint: Located in Clime 1, Sections 6 and 7. Find the southern/eastern protrusion of the Arabian Peninsula bordering the Sea of Oman.

history:
Berbera is a coastal city and was the former capital of the British Somaliland protectorate before Hargeisa. It also served as a major port of the Ifat, Adal and Isaaq sultanates from the 13th to 19th centuries.

In antiquity, Berbera was part of a chain of commercial port cities along the Somali seaboard. During the early modern period, Berbera was the most important place of trade in the Somali Peninsula.

name: Al-Daybul / Debal
history: According to modern archaeologists, Debal was founded in the first century CE, and soon became the most important trading city in Sindh. The port city was home to thousands of Sindhi sailors including the Bawarij. Ibn Hawqal, a tenth-century writer, geographer and chronicler, mentions huts of the city and the dry arid land surrounding the city that supported little agriculture. He mentions how efficiently the inhabitants of the city maintained fishing vessels and trade. The Abbasids were the first to build large stone structures including a city wall and a citadel. An earthquake in 893 AD reportedly destroyed the port city of Debal

name: Diyar Tali minhu (Yunnan / Dali)
history: Yunnan is rich in natural resources and has the largest diversity of plant life in China. Of the approximately 30,000 species of vascular plants in China, Yunnan has perhaps 17,000 or more. Yunnan's reserves of aluminium, lead, zinc and tin are the largest in China, and there are also major reserves of copper and nickel. Historically, the southwestern Silk Road to Bhitargarh in Bangladesh passed through modern Yunnan.

name: Akhmim min Sa'id Misr
history: Akhmim was known in Ancient Egypt as Ipu, Apu. In the 13th century AD, a very imposing temple still stood in Akhmim. Today, little of its past glory remains. Nothing is left of the town, the temples were almost completely dismantled, and their material was reused in the later Middle Ages. The extensive cemeteries of ancient Akhmim are yet to be fully explored. The destroyed corner of a Greco-Roman period temple with colossal statues of Ramesses II and Meritamen was discovered in 1981.

He also noted the large amount of ginger available as well as large geese and snakes. Guangzhou was visited by the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta during his journey around the world in the 14th century. He detailed the process by which the Chinese constructed their large ships in the port's shipyards.

name: Barqa (Al-Marj, Libya)
history: Barca was one of the first cities to be taken by the Arabs in 643–644 during the Islamic conquest of North Africa. It originally served as the capital of the Barqah province of the Caliphate. The city's name, Arabized as Barqah, came to refer to the former state and province of Cyrenaica. Barca remained a significant city in the tenth century under the Fatimids and Al-Bakri reports that it was a wealthy city which exported wool, honey and fruit. The attacks of Banu Hilal in the 11th century led to a sharp decline and at some point it ceased to be inhabited. When the Ottoman Turks conquered the region in 1521, they used the Turkish form "Barka" for the province, but did not retain the city's status as its capital. The Ottomans used ancient ruins as building material for a castle at the site a little before 1852, when it was visited by James Hamilton. The castle was destroyed in the 1963 Marj earthquake.
idrisiHint: North African coastal plain east of Tripoli.

name: Shīrāz min Fārs
history:
Though there is no definitive record of its existence prior to the late 7th century CE, a few archaeological finds dating from 1933 and beyond indicate that the site or vicinity of Shiraz was likely settled in the pre-Islamic era as early as the 6th century BCE.

Shiraz developed into the largest and most prosperous city of Fars and an important economic and cultural center of the caliphate. Adud al-Dawla had a large library, a hospital and several mosques, bazaars, caravanserais, palaces and gardens built in the city, while south of it he erected a fortified camp for his troops, known as Kard Fana Khusraw, in 974. One of the congregational mosques built by Adud al-Dawla has survived until the present day. Two Zoroastrian fire temples also existed in Shiraz, catering to the Persians who had not converted to Islam. One of Adud al-Dawla's palaces stretched out for nearly three miles and consisted of 360 rooms.

Birthplace of Syedna Moiyyad-al-Shirazi RA

name: Al-Fusṭāṭ min Miṣr (Old Cairo)
history:
Founded in 641 CE by ’Amr ibn al-’As following the Muslim conquest of Egypt, Fustat served as the first Islamic capital of Egypt and North Africa (Djaït, 1986; Kennedy, 2004).

Strategic Capital & Administrative Base: Originating as a garrison town (misr) adjacent to the Roman fortress of Babylon, Fustat replaced Alexandria as Egypt's political and military administrative center, serving as the launching point for further Arab expansions across North Africa.

Religious Milestone: It housed the Mosque of ’Amr ibn al-’As—the first mosque constructed on the African continent—establishing the architectural and spatial precedent for Islamic governance in Egypt.

Economic & Urban Powerhouse: Situated on the Nile, Fustat evolved into a prominent global trade and manufacturing hub. It remained Egypt’s economic engine for five centuries, laying the physical, structural, and cultural foundations for nearby Cairo, which eventually absorbed it.

Under the Fatimi Aimmat Tahereen AS (969–1171 CE), Fustat transitioned from political seat to dynamic commercial nucleus, serving as the economic engine while neighboring Cairo (al-Qahira) functioned as the royal capital.

Economic Engine: As Cairo housed the caliphs and court, Fustat remained the vibrant center of international trade, light industry, and Mediterranean-Red Sea commerce.

Industrial & Ceramic Hub: Fustat was globally famed for manufacturing high-end goods, particularly luxury lustreware ceramics (Fustat ware), glassmaking, and textiles.

Tragic Fire (1168 CE): Fustat was intentionally set ablaze for 54 days by vizier Shawar to prevent its rich resources from falling into the hands of approaching Crusaders.

During the Fatimid era, Fustat emerged as a premier center for paper trade, usage, and local rag paper production:

The Papyrus-to-Paper Shift: Under the Fatimids, affordable rag paper completely replaced papyrus and expensive parchment for daily administration, literature, and domestic business.

The Cairo Genizah: The most significant archaeological discovery regarding medieval paper occurred in Fustat’s Ben Ezra Synagogue. Jews stored discarded documents containing divine names in its genizah. Over 300,000 fragments—mostly on 10th to 13th-century rag paper—survived, giving historians an unparalleled look into everyday Fatimid society.
idrisiHint: East bank of the Nile River south of modern Cairo.

name: Samarkand
history:
Sogdian Merchant Network: Samarkand was the administrative and commercial capital of Sogdia. Sogdians were the primary merchant class of the Silk Road from the 4th to the 10th centuries, maintaining trade depots from the Mediterranean all the way into Chang'an (Xi'an), China.

Spread of Paper Technology: Tradition holds that Chinese prisoners taken after the Battle of Talas in 751 CE introduced papermaking to Samarkand; Bloom regards this as a legend and argues that paper was already known in Central Asia earlier, while still treating Samarkand as a key centre of diffusion. Samarkand paper (al-kāghadh al-samarqandī) replaced parchment and papyrus across the Abbasid administration, lowering the cost of book reproduction and accelerating the Islamic Golden Age.

name: Balkh
history:
"The Mother of Cities" (Umm al-Bilād): Ancient Bactra was one of the world's oldest urban settlements and a cradle of Zoroastrianism.

The Nawbahār Monastery & The Barmakids: Prior to the Islamic conquest, Balkh was a center of Buddhist scholarship, anchored by the  vast Nawbahār monastery. Its hereditary priestly administrators, the Pramukhas, converted to Islam and became the Barmakid family, serving as the chief viziers to Caliphs al-Mahdī and Hārūn al-Rashīd, financing translation projects, irrigation networks, and administrative offices across the Abbasid realm.

Silk Road Crossroad: Balkh commanded the southern route branching off the main east-west Silk Road, leading across the Hindu Kush into Kabul, Gandhara, and the Indus Valley.

name: Herat

It developed into a leading theological center of the early Hanafi and Karrami schools, later becoming the cultural capital of the Timurid Renaissance.

name: Merv
history:
The Oasis Hub of the Karakum: Merv’s massive multi-tiered dams on the Murghab River allowed an agricultural oasis to thrive in the desert. Without Merv, caravan travel between north-eastern Iran and Transoxiana would have been impossible.

Capital of the Caliphate under al-Maʾmūn (813–818 CE): During the Fourth Fitna, Caliph al-Maʾmūn governed the entire Abbasid Caliphate from Merv. During these five years, Merv was the administrative center of the empire, where al-Maʾmūn gathered astronomers, geographers, and translators.

Textiles & Library Collections: Famed across the Mediterranean and Asian markets for fine raw silk, silk damasks, and soft cottons. The 13th-century traveler Yāqūt al-Ḥamawī documented ten major endowed public and institutional libraries in Merv, describing them as the most extensive collections of scientific literature in the Islamic world.

name: Nishapur
history: Industrial Ceramics and Turquoise: Nishapur controlled the ancient turquoise mines of Madan, which supplied prized gemstones to both the Tang court in China and the Byzantine Empire. Excavations reveal that Nishapur was a major manufacturing center for glazed ceramic ware, known for white-slipped slipware decorated with Arabic epigraphic maxims in black Kufic script.   Intellectual Center of Khurasan: Nishapur was home to, or trained, foundational scholars across multiple disciplines: the mathematician, astronomer, and poet Omar Khayyam (who reformed the Persian solar calendar  and solved cubic equations geometrically); the theologian Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (born in Ṭūs, who studied in Nishapur); and the compiler of Hadith Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj.

name: Jurjan
history:
The Sasanian Great Wall of Gorgan: Ancient Hyrcania was shielded by the Great Wall of Gorgan (the "Red Snake"), a 195-kilometer baked-  brick barrier flanked by 38 forts, designed to defend the agrarian plains against Central Asian nomadic incursions.

Ziyarid Dynasty & The Gonbad-e Qabus: In the 10th and 11th centuries, Jurjan was the capital of the Ziyarid dynasty. The Ziyarid ruler Qābūs ibn Wushmagīr erected the Gonbad-e Qabus in 1006 CE, a 53-meter conical brick tomb-tower that survives today as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Scientific Incubator: Jurjan was where Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) taught and began writing The Canon of Medicine (al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb), and where al-Bīrūnī composed his foundational chronological text, The Remaining Signs of Past Centuries (al-Āthār al-Bāqiya).

name: Amol
history:
Capital of Autonomous Tabaristan: Amol was the primary city of Tabaristan (Mazandaran). Defended by the dense Hyrcanian rainforests and the Alborz mountains, local dynasties (such as the Bavandids and Dabuyids) maintained Persian Zoroastrian traditions for nearly two centuries after the fall of the Sasanians, later becoming a center of Zaydi Shi'ism.

Maritime and Silk Commerce: Amol operated as an inland river-port on the Haraz River near the Caspian shore. It processed raw silk, flax  textiles, and timber, serving as a maritime transshipment port connecting northern Iran with the Volga-Caspian trade route leading to the Khazar Khaganate and Kievan Rus.

Home of al-Ṭabarī: The birthplace of Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (839–923 CE), author of Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-al-Mulūk (History of the Prophets and Kings) and the monumental exegesis Jāmiʿ al-Bayān.

name: Daylam and Gilan
history:
Highland Autonomy & Military Dominance: The Daylamites were mountain warriors who used their terrain to resist foreign invasion. They were armed with heavy painted shields and their signature two- pronged javelins (zhūpīn).

The Buyid Dynasty & The Ikhwān al-Ṣafā: In the 10th century—the era in which the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafā were written—the Daylamite Buyid (Buwayhid) Dynasty swept down from these mountains, conquered western Iran, and seized Baghdad in 945 CE. The Buyids ruled as Shāhanshāhs, reducing the Sunni Caliph to a religious figurehead. The philosophical society of the Ikhwān al-Ṣafā operated within this cosmopolitan, Shi'i-leaning Buyid environment.

Raw Silk Trade: Gilan produced high-grade raw silk (qazz), which was spun in the workshops of Rayy, Baghdad, and Aleppo.

name: Isfahan
history:
The Twin Cities (Jayy & al-Yahūdiyya): Isfahan originally comprised two settlements: Jayy, a fortified round administrative citadel, and al-Yahūdiyya, a commercial and artisan settlement founded by Jewish exiles. Over centuries, they merged to form the urban core of Isfahan.

Agricultural Wealth & Industrial Weaving: Located in an oasis fed by the Zayandeh River, Isfahan was famous for cotton, fruit orchards, and saffron. Its textile artisans produced ʿAttābī (watered-silk/taffeta) and linen fabrics exported throughout the Islamic world.

Kakuyid Capital & Avicenna’s Last Patron: Under the Kakuyid emir ʿAlāʾ al-Dawla, Isfahan was an intellectual hub. Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) spent the last 14 years of his life here, completing (it was begun earlier, in the Ray/Hamadan period) his philosophical encyclopedia Kitāb al-Shifāʾ (The Book of Healing).

name: Hamadan
history:
Ancient Ecbatana: Hamadan is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities. It served as the capital of the Median Empire (Hagmatāna) and the summer capital of the Achaemenid Persian kings.

The Gatehouse of the Great Khurasan Road: Hamadan held a strategic position in western Iran. All commercial traffic traveling between the Mesopotamian lowlands (Ctesiphon, later Baghdad) and the Silk Road of Central Asia had to pass through the Zagros gates via Hulwan and Asadabad directly into Hamadan.

Tomb of Avicenna: In the 11th century, Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) served as vizier to the Buyid amir Shams al-Dawla of Hamadan. He composed portions of his philosophical and medical works here, died in the city in 1037 CE, and his mausoleum remains a cultural landmark in Hamadan today.

name: Baghdad
history:
Imperial Capital of the Abbasid Caliphate: Founded in 762 CE by Caliph al-Manṣūr as a planned circular fortress-city (Madīnat al-Salām). Baghdad grew into an imperial metropolis with over one million inhabitants.

The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Ḥikma) & Translation Movement: Under Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Maʾmūn, Baghdad was the intellectual capital of the medieval world. State-sponsored translation circles converted Greek, Syriac, Sanskrit, and Middle Persian texts into Arabic, catalyzing foundational advances in algebra (al-Khwārizmī), philosophy (al-Kindī), astronomy, and medicine.

Global Entrepôt: Positioned along the Tigris, Baghdad controlled both river traffic flowing down to Basra and the Persian Gulf maritime routes (to India and China), and the overland caravan routes leading east to Central Asia and west to Syria and Egypt.

name: Mosul
history:
"The Junction Point" (al-Mawṣil): The name al-Mawṣil means "the linking point," identifying its role bridging Upper Mesopotamia (al- Jazīra) with Lower Iraq, Syria, and the mountainous approaches to Armenia and Azerbaijan.

The Muslin Misconception & Etymological Origin: Muslin fabric did not originate in Mosul; it originated in Bengal (modern-day Bangladesh and West Bengal, India), where it was spun from the indigenous tree cotton Gossypium arboreum into ultra-fine gossamer weaves. However, the fabric acquired its global trade name—"muslin"(French: mousseline; Italian: mussolina)—because Western European merchants knew fine cotton cloth from Mosul and named it after the city; Marco Polo describes the cloth called “mosolin” as made at Mosul.

name: Aleppo

name: Ītil / Atil
history:
Following the Arab-Khazar wars and the vulnerability of Balanjar/Samandar in the Caucasus, the Khagan moved the imperial administrative center northward to Itil along the Volga estuary.

Itil was a tripartite city split by the river branches: Khamlīj / Sarighshin on the western bank (mercantile, inhabited by Muslims, Christians, and pagan Slavs/Turks) and the Khagan's walled brick island fortress (Jazīrah) on the eastern branch.

The pivot of the Volga Trade Route, connecting the Abbasid Caliphate and Central Asian Samanids with Northern Europe and Scandinavia (the Varangians/Rus). Hundreds of thousands of Abbasid silver dirhams found in Baltic hoards passed through Itil.

The administrative heart where the Khazar ruling elite converted to Judaism in the 8th–9th centuries.

Sacked by Sviatoslav I of Kiev in 968 or 969 CE, ending Khazar hegemony. The urban nucleus was later succeeded by the trading emporium of Saksin in the 11th–12th centuries, and subsequently Sarai Batu (the Golden Horde capital) further upstream.

The Volga Delta remains the exit point of Russia's primary inland waterway into the Caspian Basin.

Astrakhan operates as the primary northern hub of the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC) linking Russia, Iran, and India.

The Volga Delta is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, renowned for sturgeon spawning and extensive wetland biodiversity.

Resolving the exact boundaries of the Khazar capital remains one of Eurasian archaeology's most active research questions, using satellite imagery and paleohydrological modeling of fluctuating medieval Caspian water levels

name: Bulghār / Bolghar
history:
Capital of Volga Bulgaria: From the 10th century onwards, Bolghar served as the primary political, economic, and religious center of Volga Bulgaria, alternating administrative roles intermittently with the interior fortress of Bilyar.

Adoption of Islam (922 CE): Volga Bulgaria adopted Islam as its state religion in 922 CE under ruler Almış (Jaʿfar ibn ʿAbdallāh), following the official diplomatic mission from the Abbasid Caliph al-Muqtadir, documented in detail by embassy secretary Ahmad ibn Fadlan.

Northern Trade Emporium: Bolghar functioned as the furthest northern hub of the medieval Islamic trade route along the Volga, exchanging furs, walrus ivory, wax, honey, and amber from Scandinavia and the Taiga with silver dirhams, silk, and spices from the Abbasid and Samanid realms.

Mongol Conquest & Golden Horde: Sacked by Batu Khan during the Mongol invasion in 1236, the city was rebuilt under the Golden Horde (Ulus of Jochi) and served as an early regional center and minting hub before power shifted north toward Kazan.

name: Kuyāba / Kyiv
history:
Center of Kievan Rus': In early Islamic geography (drawing on the 10th-century accounts of al-Balkhī, al-Iṣṭakhrī, and Ibn Ḥawqal), the Rus were described as having three main centers: Kūyāba (Kyiv), Ṣalāw (identifiable with Novgorod/Ilmen Slavs), and Arthāniyyah (often associated with ancient Rostov/Timeryovo). Among these, Kuyāba was noted as the primary trade gateway accessible to travelers from the Muslim world and the Byzantine Empire.

Trade Route from the Varangians to the Greeks: Kyiv was the linchpin of the major medieval river highway linking Scandinavia and the Baltic Sea directly to Constantinople via the Dnieper and the Black Sea.

Christianization of Kievan Rus' (988 CE): Under Grand Prince Vladimir the Great (Volodymyr), Kyiv became the spiritual and political cradle of East Slavic Orthodox Christianity following the mass baptism of its citizens in the Dnieper.

Mongol Sack (1240): Sacked and largely leveled during the Mongol invasion under Batu Khan in 1240, after which political primacy fragmented across northern principalities and Halych-Volhynia.

name: Samandar
history:
Early Khazar Capital: Samandar served as a Khazar capital from the 720s, after Balanjar, before the administrative center moved northward to Atil (Itil) in the Volga delta between about 730 and 750 CE.

Arab–Khazar Wars: During the early 8th century, particularly during the campaigns of the Umayyad generals al-Jarrah ibn Abdallah and Marwan ibn Muhammad (the future Caliph Marwan II) around 722–737 CE, Samandar was captured by Arab forces. This southward vulnerability forced the Khazars to shift their royal court to the more defensible northern marshes of the lower Volga.

Viticulture and Trade Center: Classical Arab geographers (such as al-Iṣṭakhrī and Ibn Ḥawqal) described Samandar as a wealthy, thriving trading city filled with thousands of vineyards and gardens, with a mixed population of Muslims, Christians, Jews, and pagans, complete with mosques, churches, and synagogues.

Destruction by Sviatoslav: Like Atil and Sarkel, Samandar was sacked and devastated during the campaigns of the Kievan Rus' prince Sviatoslav I in 965–969 CE, an event recorded by Ibn Ḥawqal as having destroyed the city's famous vineyards.

name: Tūlī / Thule
history:
Pytheas's Voyage (c. 325 BCE): Pytheas sailed north from Massalia (modern Marseille) past Britain, reporting an island six days' sail north of Britain where the midsummer sun did not set and the sea became a slush-like substance ("sea-lung").

Ptolemaic Benchmark of Latitude: Claudius Ptolemy used Thule in his Geographia as the parallel of 63° N, setting the absolute northern boundary of his known world and the baseline for calculating the width of the northern climata.

Adoption in Islamic Geodesy & Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ: Medieval Islamic geographers and astronomers (including al-Battānī, al-Bīrūnī, and the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ) preserved this Ptolemaic coordinate framework. Tūlī was regularly cited in the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ to demonstrate the extreme variations of solar declination, where nights shrink to zero during the summer solstice and daylight disappears during the winter solstice.

Metaphorical Concept (Ultima Thule): In Latin literature (Virgil, Seneca) and medieval cartography, Ultima Thule became a proverbial expression denoting any distant, unknown goal beyond the borders of the known world.

name: Bilād al-Ṣaqālibah
history:
Ethnonym & Scope in Arabic Sources: The Arabic term Ṣiqlāb (singular) / Ṣaqālibah (plural) derives via Byzantine Greek Sklávoi (Σκλάβοι) / Sklabēnoí (Σκλαβηνοί). In early sources (such as Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Ibn Rustah, and al-Iṣṭakhrī), it specifically designated the sedentary agricultural Slavs of Eastern and Central Europe, distinguishing them from the nomadic steppe Turks (Pechenegs, Khazars) and the maritime Scandinavian Norsemen (Rūs / Varangians).

The Trans-Eurasian Slave and Fur Trade: Bilād al-Ṣaqālibah was a primary supplier in the medieval Eurasian trade network:

Merchants, notably the Radhanites and Varangian traders, transported amber, wax, luxury furs, and Slavic captives along river routes into the Islamic world.

In the Islamic Mediterranean and Abbasid Caliphate, captive Europeans became prominent administrative and military figures known collectively as the Saqaliba (serving notably in Umayyad Córdoba, the Fatimid Caliphate, and North Africa).

Ibn Faḍlān's Account (921–922 CE): Ahmad ibn Fadlan referred to Almış, the ruler of Volga Bulgaria, as the "King of the Ṣaqālibah" (Malik al-Ṣaqālibah), reflecting the broad use of the term in Baghdad to denote northern European rulers and their diverse subjects.

In traditional seven-clime cosmology, its core and northern reaches are placed squarely within the Sixth and Seventh Climes (al-Iqlīm al-Sādis wa-al-Sābiʿ).

name: Bilād al-Khazar
history:
Eurasian Steppe Empire (c. 650–969 CE): The Khazar Khaganate emerged as a successor state to the Western Turkic Khaganate (Göktürks), forging a powerful nomadic-sedentary confederation that ruled the strategic corridor between the Black and Caspian seas for over three centuries.

During the 7th and 8th centuries, the Khazar armies checked the northward expansion of the Umayyad and early Abbasid Caliphates during the fierce Arab–Khazar Wars, preventing Arab armies from consolidating control north of the Greater Caucasus.

The Khazars formed close diplomatic and dynastic alliances with the Byzantine Empire (providing emperors such as Justinian II and Constantine V with Khazar royal brides; Emperor Leo IV was known as "Leo the Khazar").

Conversion to Judaism: Sometime in the 8th or early 9th century, the Khazar ruling royalty and core nobility adopted Judaism, making Khazaria a unique Jewish-led medieval empire whose religious and political structure was discussed across Islamic, Byzantine, and Hebrew texts (most famously in the 10th-century Khazar Correspondence and Judah Halevi’s Kuzari).

Crossroads of Trans-Eurasian Commerce: Khazaria dominated the northern terminus of the Silk Road and the Volga trade route. The Khagan levied customs duties (ushr) on goods passing between China, Central Asia, the Islamic Caliphate, Kievan Rus', and Scandinavia.

Fall of the Khaganate: In 965–969 CE, Grand Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev launched a massive military expedition down the Don and Volga rivers, sacking Sarkel, Atil, and Samandar, which permanently shattered Khazar central authority.

In the Rasāʾil, the northern steppe marches and upper reaches of the Volga are traditionally grouped under the Seventh Clime (al-Iqlīm al-Sābiʿ), while in al-Idrīsī’s detailed cartographic division, the core territory spans across the boundary of the Sixth Clime, Section 6 (al-Iqlīm al-Sādis, al-Juzʾ al-Sādis) and reaches into the Seventh Clime, Sections 5 and 6.

name: Bilād Yājūj wa-Mājūj
history:
Eschatological Role in Islamic Cosmology: In the Qurʾān (Surah al-Kahf 18:93–99 and Surah al-Anbiyāʾ 21:96), Dhū al-Qarnayn constructs an iron and molten-copper barrier between two mountain ridges (al-Saddayn) to protect a vulnerable population from the destructive raids of Yājūj and Mājūj. Their breaking through the barrier is prophesied as one of the major signs of the end of time (Ashrāṭ al-Sāʿah).

Following a nightmare by the Abbasid Caliph al-Wāthiq in which the barrier was breached, the court interpreter Sallām al-Tarjumān was dispatched on an imperial diplomatic expedition to find and inspect the rampart.

Sallām’s itinerary—recorded by Ibn Khordadbeh and later synthesized by al-Idrīsī—took him from Samarra through the Caucasus, Khazaria, and Central Asian steppe routes all the way to a great fortified mountain gateway in the east, which he reported was intact.

Association with Steppe Nomads: Classical Arab, Persian, and Syriac authors frequently associated Yājūj and Mājūj ethnographically with the fierce pastoral nomad confederations of inner and northern Eurasia (Scythians, Huns, Turks, and later the Mongols).

In the traditional seven-clime system, this wild, mountainous northern redoubt is set in the far northeastern quadrant of the Seventh Clime (al-Iqlīm al-Sābiʿ), extending across the border of the Sixth Clime.

name: Bilād al-Kīmāk
history:
The Kimek–Kipchak Confederation (c. 880–1035 CE): Following the collapse of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 CE, seven tribes—including the Kimeks, Kipchaks, Eymür, Tatars, and Bayandur—formed a centralized tribal khaganate headed by the Kimek ruler (the Khagan).

Semi-Sedentary Culture and Literacy: While primarily pastoral nomads famous for horse breeding and cattle herding, geographers like al-Idrīsī, Gardīzī, and Abū Dulaf emphasized that the Kimeks maintained fortified towns, iron and gold metallurgy, stone castles, and agricultural irrigation along the Irtysh. They also used the Old Turkic script written on reeds, as confirmed by archaeological finds of inscribed bronze mirrors in the Irtysh and Tarbagatai regions.

Ancestor of the Kipchak/Cuman Expansion: In the 11th century, internal shifts and migrations (spurred by the westward movement of the Qun and Khitans) led to the decline of the central Kimek authority. name: Bilād al-Jazāʾir
history:
Island Capital of the Khazars: In classical Arabic accounts (such as those of Ibn Rustah, al-Iṣṭakhrī, and al-Masʿūdī), the Khazar capital of Itil was described as being divided by the river branches into multiple island sectors. The royal palace and brick castle of the Khagan were built specifically on a large island (al-Jazīrah) protected by surrounding river moats and reed beds.

Natural Fortress and Transit Chokepoint: The dense labyrinth of delta islands served as a natural defensive refuge and maritime gateway. Control over these islands allowed the Khazars, and later the Golden Horde and the Astrakhan Khanate, to monitor and tax all riverine and maritime traffic passing between the Russian interior, the Caspian Sea, and the Silk Road networks.

The Successor Cities of Saksin and Xacitarxan: Following the fall of the Khazar capital in the late 10th century, the island delta became the site of Saksin (a major 11th–13th-century Oghuz/Kipchak trading emporium) and subsequently Xacitarxan (medieval Astrakhan), which served as an essential hub of the Golden Horde.

paragraphs: Ecological Reserve & Biosphere: The Volga Delta is home to the Astrakhan Nature Reserve (established in 1919 and designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve), world-famous for its extensive fields of Caspian lotus (Nelumbo caspica), critical migratory bird habitats, and primary spawning grounds for endangered Caspian sturgeon.

Strategic Maritime Gateway: The delta branches accommodate the Volga–Caspian Shipping Canal, serving as Russia’s primary maritime outlet to the Caspian Sea and a central nexus of the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC).

name: Juzur Baḥr Jurjān
history:
Naval Raids and Pirates of Gorgan: Medieval historians such as Ibn Isfandiyar and al-Masʿūdī record that the Caspian islands—particularly those around the Bay of Gorgan and Cheleken—served as maritime shelters, staging bases, and navigational shelters for local Daylamite, Tabari, and later Rus' naval fleets during the Caspian expeditions of the Rus (9th–10th centuries).

Naphtha and Mineral Extraction: As early as the 10th-century writings of al-Iṣṭakhrī and Ibn Ḥawqal, the eastern islands and coastal tongues (especially Cheleken) were famous for surface oil seepages and raw naphtha (naft) extraction, which was collected, barreled, and shipped across the Caspian for burning and military use.

19th-Century Russo-Persian Geopolitics: Ashuradeh Island played a pivotal diplomatic and strategic role in modern history. In 1838, the Russian Empire occupied Ashuradeh to suppress Turkmen piracy in the Bay of Gorgan, establishing a permanent Russian naval station and coaling depot there until the 1921 Russo-Persian Treaty recognized Iranian sovereignty over the island.

paragraphs: In classical Arabic and Persian geography—including Ptolemy’s Geographia, al-Khwārizmī’s Kitāb Ṣūrat al-Arḍ, the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, and al-Idrīsī—Baḥr Jurjān (بحر جرجان, the Sea of Gorgan / Hyrcanian Sea) is one of the standard medieval names for the Caspian Sea (alternatively called Baḥr al-Khazar, Baḥr Ṭabaristān, or Baḥr Qazwīn).
Juzur Baḥr Jurjān (جزر بحر جرجان, "The Islands of the Sea of Gorgan") refers to the coastal barrier islands, sandspits, and archipelagos located inside the Caspian basin.

paragraphs: Ashuradeh & Miankaleh Peninsula: Part of the UNESCO-designated Miankaleh Biosphere Reserve and a Ramsar wetland site, serving as a wintering habitat for millions of migratory birds (such as flamingos, pelicans, and swans) and one of the last major refuges of the endangered Caspian seal (Pusa caspica).

name: Marāghah / Maragheh
history:
Pre-Islamic and Early Islamic Foundation: Known in early Persian accounts as Akra-rudh or Afrazah-rudh ("river of Afrah"), Maragheh has long been associated by historical topographers with Phraaspa or Phraata, the winter capital of ancient Atropatene. During the early Abbasid period, it was fortified by order of Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

First Capital of the Ilkhanate (1256–1265 CE): Following the Mongol conquest of West Asia, Hulagu Khan chose Maragheh as the first official capital of the Ilkhanate Empire before the administrative court was moved to Tabriz.

Founded in 1259 CE under the patronage of Hulagu Khan and directed by the polymath Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Maragheh was the site of the most advanced astronomical observatory of the medieval world.

It hosted international scholars (including Byzantine and Chinese mathematicians) and housed a library containing hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

The mathematical and geometric models developed here—most notably the Tusi couple and alternative non-Ptolemaic planetary systems created by al-Tusi, Muʾayyad al-Din al-ʿUrdi, and Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi—laid crucial groundwork that influenced later Renaissance astronomy, including Nicolaus Copernicus.

Seljuk and Ilkhanid Architecture: The city is celebrated for its five monumental medieval memorial towers (gonbads), including the Seljuk-era Gonbad-e Sorkh (Red Dome, built in 1147 CE, a landmark of Iranian decorative brickwork) and the Gonbad-e Ghaffariyeh.

historySections.title: Identity in the journal

name: Jabal Bāb al-Abwāb / Derbent
history:
The Sasanian Wall of Derbent: Built primarily under Sasanian emperors Kavad I and Khosrow I Anushirvan (6th century CE), Derbent was engineered to seal off the narrow Caspian gates against incursions by northern nomadic peoples (Huns, Sabirs, and later Khazars). The stone fortifications included:

The citadel of Naryn-Kala overlooking the heights.

Two parallel stone walls (the northern and southern city walls) running 3 km from the mountain crest directly into the sea, enclosing the medieval city.

The Dag-Bary (Mountain Wall), an extensive stone rampart that originally extended over 40 km westward into the impassable Caucasus peaks.

Arab Conquest & The "Gate of Gates": Captured in 642–643 CE by Arab armies under Suraqa ibn Amr and Salman ibn Rabi'a, the city was renamed Bāb al-Abwāb ("The Gate of Gates") or simply al-Bāb. It served for two centuries as the primary military garrison, fortress, and staging ground for the Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates during the protracted Arab–Khazar Wars.

The Emirate of Derbent & The Shirvanshahs: From 869 CE onwards, the autonomous Emirate of Derbent (ruled by the Arab Hashimid dynasty) governed the strategic fortress, maintaining a maritime port and frontier trading post before being absorbed into the realm of the Shirvanshahs and later the Seljuks and Ilkhanids.

The Derbent Juma Mosque: Founded in 733–734 CE by Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, it is the oldest active mosque within the territory of the Russian Federation and one of the earliest preserved Islamic religious structures in the Caucasus.

name: Bījār / Bayḥar
history:
Sasanian Foundation: Tradition attributes the founding of Baylaqān (Paytakaran) to Sasanian King Qubadh I (Kavad I), who established it as a strategic fortified outpost guarding the Transcaucasian frontier.

Arab Conquest & Trade: Captured during the early Muslim conquest of the Caucasus (c. 645 CE) by Salman ibn Rabi'a, Baylaqān developed into a prosperous trading emporium and agricultural hub on the southern border of Arran, renowned for its irrigation canals (Nahr Qubādh), pomegranates, and textile manufacturing.

The Mongol Sack (1221 CE): During the initial reconnaissance expedition of Jebe and Subutai into the Caucasus in 1221 CE, Baylaqān refused to surrender and was besieged, captured, and comprehensively destroyed by the Mongols, with much of its population slaughtered.

Rebuilding by Timur (1403 CE): In 1403 CE, Timur (Tamerlane) ordered the complete reconstruction of Baylaqān’s city walls and the re-excavation of its primary Barlas irrigation canal from the Aras River, though the city declined into ruin following his death.

Historical Fortress & Garrisons: Recorded historically in Safavid and Qajar chronicles as an important frontier stronghold of the Garrus district, governed by local Kurdish and Turkic emirs.

Textile & Carpet Tradition: Celebrated across Persian artistic history for its distinct, heavy, tightly knotted Bijar rugs (known internationally as the "Iron Rugs of Persia" due to their durable weave).

paragraphs: In classical Arabic and Persian geography—including the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Ibn Khordadbeh, al-Iṣṭakhrī, Ibn Ḥawqal, and al-Idrīsī—the toponym appears with clerical orthographic variations (often due to unpointed Arabic script: بيجر / بيحر / بيلقان / بيلكان). In medieval geographic texts, this entry most prominently corresponds to Baylaqān (بيلقان), the historic fortified frontier city of the Mil steppe in the Arran region (modern Azerbaijan Republic), with a secondary candidate being Bījār (بيجار) in the Jibal/Kurdistan frontier (modern Iran).

name: Bilād Haqṭah min al-Rūm
history:
1. Western Gothia (Septimania / Southern France)

Last Redoubt of the Visigothic Kingdom: Following the defeat of Alaric II by Clovis I at the Battle of Vouillé (507 CE), Septimania was the sole Gallic territory retained by the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo, earning it the contemporary Latin name Gothia.

Umayyad Frontier & Carolingian Reconquest: During the early 8th century, Arab and Berber armies under al-Samh ibn Malik crossed the Pyrenees and incorporated Septimania into al-Andalus, ruling from Narbonne (Arbūnah) until Pepin the Short conquered the region in 759 CE. Under Charlemagne, the territory was organized as the March of Gothia (Marca Gothica), governed by the Margraves of Gothia.

Flourishing Jewish & Cultural Hub: During the medieval period, the cities of Gothia (notably Narbonne, Lunel, and Montpellier) hosted renowned Jewish academies and served as a vital intellectual bridge translating scientific and philosophical works between Arabic, Hebrew, and Latin.

2. Eastern Gothia (Crimea)

Surviving Gothic Enclave: After the migration period, a population of Ostrogoths settled in the Crimean Mountains, retaining their Germanic dialect (Crimean Gothic) well into early modern times.

Byzantine Dependency & Khazar Wars: The Crimean Goths maintained close alliances with the Byzantine Empire, being organized ecclesiastically under the Metropolitanate of Gothia of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople. In the 8th century, they led an uprising against Khazar dominance under John of Gothia.

Principality of Theodoro: In the late Middle Ages, Crimean Gothia crystallized into the Christian Principality of Theodoro based at the mountain citadel of Mangup, surviving until its conquest by the Ottoman Empire in 1475.
